title: The ETF Review: MTUM Is a Semiconductor Bet in a Momentum Wrapper
subtitle: BlackRock’s flagship factor strategy trades like a chip portfolio with an index rule that caps its own upside
summary: The iShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF promises systematic exposure to market winners, but rigid quarterly turnover caps and heavy sector concentration turn it into a disguised tech trade. Investors paying for quantitative discipline instead receive a whipsaw-prone portfolio that historically lags simpler momentum rivals.

bodyHtml:
You think you bought a clever mathematical mirror of the American stock market. You bought an algorithm that reads the tape, finds the fastest runners, and rents them until they tire. That is the marketing pitch behind momentum investing, after all: cut the losers, ride the winners, repeat.

Look under the hood of the iShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF, ticker MTUM, and you will find something else entirely. You did not buy a cross-section of Wall Street's winners. You bought a heavily concentrated bet on the semiconductor cycle, disguised as a diversified factor strategy, padded with a bizarre handful of defensive dividend aristocrats.

When chips rip, MTUM looks like pure genius. When the semiconductor complex rolls over, the fund does not hedge, pivot, or dodge. It simply absorbs the hit, waits for a scheduled calendar date, and mechanically dumps the wreckage after the damage has already occurred.

Worse, the fund is shrinking at a breathtaking pace. At the end of July 2026, MTUM held roughly $25.15 billion in net assets. By late October, assets had dropped to about $18.1 billion. That is a 28% decline in three months.

Over that exact same stretch, the fund’s share price was roughly flat, gaining about 1%. The market did not shrink this fund. Investors took six to seven billion dollars and walked out the door. To understand why institutional money is leaving, you have to look at what MTUM actually holds and how its own rulebook trips it up.

What You Actually Own

On paper, MTUM owns 125 large- and mid-cap American equities selected from the broad MSCI USA universe. In practice, third-party counts show about 129 actual holdings due to representative sampling. But the return of this fund is decided by a tiny handful of names.

As of late October 2026, the top ten holdings account for 35.2% of the fund. Leading the roster is AMD at 5.84%, followed by Micron Technology at 4.95%, Intel at 3.84%, and Cisco Systems at 3.67%. Palo Alto Networks, Alphabet, Applied Materials, and Sandisk also claim outsized positions. Five semiconductor companies—AMD, Micron, Intel, Applied Materials, and Sandisk—make up roughly 19.5% of the entire portfolio. Throw in Marvell Technology and Lam Research, and the chip complex easily exceeds 23%.

Sector weights tell an even starker story. Information Technology stands at 54.6% of the portfolio. Industrials follow at 10.1%, Health Care at 9.4%, and Energy at 8.5%. The top four sectors alone make up 82.6% of the fund. Compare that to late July, when technology stood at 47.6%. Between the scheduled August portfolio review and organic market drift, MTUM did not diversify away from tech; it dove deeper in.

Then comes the ballast. Tucked between hyper-volatile chip designers and networking firms sit Johnson & Johnson at 3.48%, Exxon Mobil at 3.09%, and Coca-Cola at 2.05%, alongside Merck and Chevron. These companies are not tearing up the tape. They appear in the portfolio because the index screens for risk-adjusted performance rather than raw speed. A steady utility-like stock with subdued volatility can score higher than a volatile rocket ship.

The result is a portfolio with a split personality. It pairs an aggressive, highly cyclical hardware bet with defensive consumer staples and oil producers.

When the trade works, it produces blistering performance. In April 2026, during a dramatic semiconductor melt-up, Intel jumped 114%, AMD gained 74%, Sandisk surged 73%, and Micron rose 53%. MTUM rode that wave to a first-half gain exceeding 37%.

Then came July. The chip rally broke. Micron, AMD, and Intel plunged between 18% and 36% in a matter of weeks. MTUM immediately became the worst-performing factor ETF on the board, trailing standard low-volatility strategies by more than 14 percentage points in a single month. In October, while the broader market gained about 1%, MTUM dropped roughly 4.6%. The fund sits about 12% below its 52-week high, trapped in the very cyclicality it was supposed to outmaneuver.

How the Sausage Is Made

To understand how an algorithm ends up loading half its money into tech, you have to examine the index. MTUM does not track the plain MSCI USA Momentum Index. Since November 2020, it has tracked the MSCI USA Momentum SR Variant Index.

BlackRock manages the fund using physical representative sampling rather than full replication. The managers must invest at least 80% of assets in index components, leaving up to 20% for futures, options, cash, or non-index securities. The fund also engages in securities lending, loaning out up to one-third of its assets to generate marginal income. A subtle tax wrinkle lurks here: substitute payments received in lieu of real dividends on lent shares do not count as qualified dividend income, carrying a slightly higher tax burden for taxable accounts.

The index selects the top 125 securities using a momentum score based on price returns over two distinct timeframes: the past six months and the past twelve months. In both cases, the index deliberately skips the most recent month to avoid short-term reversals. It then subtracts the local risk-free interest rate to isolate excess return.

Crucially, the index divides that excess return by the stock’s three-year annualized volatility of weekly returns. This measures risk-adjusted momentum. A volatile stock that doubled might receive a lower score than a sleepy stock that gained 15% with zero turbulence. The six- and twelve-month scores are standardized as z-scores, blended 50/50, and capped at positive or negative three.

Here lies a mathematical quirk. If a stock earns a positive z-score, its weighting multiplier is calculated as one plus the score. If a stock receives a negative z-score, its multiplier becomes one minus the score. Negative scores are not zeroed out; they are mathematically inverted into positive numbers, occasionally yielding surprisingly heavy weights for lagging names that experienced sudden drops in volatility.

Once scores are tallied, they are multiplied by each company's ordinary market capitalization. Cap-weighting, where bigger companies receive larger shares of the fund simply because of their size, is preserved here with a momentum tilt. Individual issuers are capped at 5%, while groups of affiliated companies above 5% cannot exceed 25% in aggregate.

Rebalancing happens quarterly, at the close of the final business day of February, May, August, and November. MTUM shifted to this quarterly schedule in February 2024, well before the broader MSCI momentum index family adopted it. Anyone telling you this fund updates twice a year is relying on an obsolete rulebook.

Yet the defining feature of MTUM is not its math score. It is the turnover cap.

The index enforces a hard 30% one-way turnover limit per quarterly reconstitution. If the raw momentum rankings dictate replacing 45% of the portfolio, the algorithm is forbidden from doing so. It adds the highest-ranked newcomers and drops the lowest-ranked incumbents, re-evaluates the math, and trims the trades until total turnover slips under 30%.

Think of MTUM as a sports car fitted with a mechanical speed limiter. The engine can detect the open road, but the governor refuses to let it accelerate past a pre-set velocity. Because the 30% turnover constraint binds in most quarters, the fund is deliberately prohibited from fully expressing its own quantitative signals. The rule was designed to prevent excessive trading costs, but it leaves MTUM perpetually holding yesterday's winners long after their momentum has died.

The Bill

On surface expenses, MTUM looks remarkably cheap. Its expense ratio—the annual management fee deducted directly from fund assets—is just 0.15%. That works out to $15 a year on a $10,000 investment, or about $150 over a decade before compounding.

The fund is also operationally liquid. Its 30-day median bid/ask spread—the trading gap between what buyers offer and sellers demand—is razor-thin at 0.03%, or three basis points. It routinely trades at virtually zero premium or discount to its net asset value (NAV), meaning you can get in and out at fair intrinsic value without friction. Average daily trading volume runs near one million shares.

Management fees and trading spreads are not what cost MTUM investors money. The actual penalty arrives via tracking difference and taxes.

Tracking difference measures how closely the fund’s actual performance mirrors the paper index it tracks. Over one year, MTUM trailed its benchmark index by 19 basis points. Over three- and ten-year periods, the drag averaged 21 basis points annually. On a 0.15% headline expense ratio, losing an additional six basis points a year to sampling frictions and transaction costs adds up.

The real damage happens in taxable brokerage accounts. ETFs typically offer superior tax efficiency through the creation/redemption process, where specialized market makers swap baskets of underlying shares for ETF units in-kind, avoiding realized capital gains. But MTUM experienced a dizzying 104% portfolio turnover for the fiscal year ended July 31, 2026, after churning through 116% the year prior. Replacing the entire portfolio once a year generates unavoidable tax friction.

Look at the issuer's own published returns as of September 30, 2026. Over ten years, MTUM delivered an annualized NAV return of 16.48%. After accounting for taxes on distributions, that return slipped slightly to 16.16%. But for an investor who sold the position at the end of ten years, the annualized after-tax return cratered to 13.94%.

That is a 2.54 percentage point penalty every single year. On a real position, giving up two and a half percentage points annually turns a $10,000 initial investment into roughly $37,000 instead of nearly $46,000. MTUM's high turnover leaves a paper trail that the tax code ruthlessly punishes.

The Scoreboard

Against standard benchmarks and direct rivals, MTUM’s historical record reveals deep structural trade-offs.

Through the end of the third quarter of 2026, the fund's official numbers looked formidable on a nominal basis. NAV total return ran 27.2% year to date, 24.4% over one year, and 32.4% annualized over three years, easing to 13.8% over five years and 16.5% over ten. Its benchmark posted nearly identical figures across every window, which tells you the fund tracks its own index closely.

Then bring in the competition. MTUM’s primary rival is the Invesco S&P 500 Momentum ETF, ticker SPMO. SPMO charges a slightly lower 0.13% expense ratio and manages about $22 billion. But the engineering under SPMO’s hood is completely different.

SPMO tracks the S&P 500 Momentum Index, which selects roughly 100 names using simple 12-month trailing returns adjusted for daily volatility. It ignores mid-caps entirely. More importantly, SPMO rebalances only twice a year, in March and September, and uses a generous 20% rank buffer. Under this buffer rule, an existing stock does not get booted just because another name nudged past it. It must fall significantly down the rankings before SPMO cuts it loose.

The consequence of that design is striking. SPMO’s turnover runs at just 44%—less than half of MTUM’s 104% churn.

Through late October 2026, MTUM and SPMO showed nearly identical year-to-date total returns of 21.4% and 21.5%, comfortably ahead of the broad market S&P 500 ETF (SPY) at 13.9%. But expand the timeline and MTUM's performance deteriorates.

Over five years, MTUM compounded at an annualized 11.4%. SPMO gained 19.1% annualized, while the basic S&P 500 gained 12.7%. MTUM actually lagged the unmanaged broad market over five years, while its direct momentum rival outperformed by more than six percentage points a year.

Over ten years, the gap is just as stark. MTUM delivered an annualized 16.1%, while SPMO compounded at 19.8%. The broad S&P 500 returned 15.5%. That near four-point annual gap over a decade is the difference between growing your capital roughly 4.5 times over versus about six times over. A sector-neutral alternative like JPMorgan's JMOM, which charges 0.12%, also outpaced MTUM over five years at 13.2% annualized, proving that you did not need a giant semiconductor overweight to generate respectable factor alpha.

Today, MTUM trades at a trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) multiple of about 26x, compared to roughly 24.5x for the S&P 500. A P/E multiple tells you how many dollars investors are willing to pay for one dollar of trailing corporate earnings; higher numbers imply higher expectations. Given that technology makes up more than half the portfolio, a 26x multiple seems modest. That discount exists solely because slow-growing ballast like Exxon and J&J pulls down the aggregate valuation. The portfolio offers a minimal dividend yield of 0.6%, carrying an aggressive three-year beta of 1.27 and an annualized standard deviation of 20.4%. Beta measures volatility relative to the market: a beta of 1.27 means that when the broader market moves 10%, MTUM typically moves nearly 13%.

This is not a defensive strategy. It is high-octane exposure that has systematically struggled to beat its simpler peers.

The Bear Case

The core case against MTUM is that its mathematical architecture is engineered to stumble during market rotations.

In their 2016 Journal of Financial Economics study, Kent Daniel and Tobias Moskowitz named the phenomenon "momentum crashes." Momentum strategies do not fail randomly; they experience catastrophic drawdowns during abrupt market inflection points. Daniel and Moskowitz documented that in the three months following the Great Financial Crisis trough, from March to May 2009, past market losers surged 163% while past winners gained just 8%.

The authors showed that fourteen of the fifteen worst momentum months in modern history followed multi-year market downturns. Every single one of them happened in months when the broader market was rising. The crash is not a slow bleed. It is a violent rotation upward into beaten-down junk—a move that a long-only fund holding yesterday’s winners cannot participate in. Because MTUM cannot short the laggards, it absorbs the downside of its existing positions while missing the initial surge of the new market leaders.

Factor crowding dramatically compounds this danger. In a 2020 paper titled "Zooming In on Equity Factor Crowding," quantitative researcher Jean-Philippe Bouchaud and his co-authors demonstrated that momentum rebalancing accounts for an estimated 1% to 2% of total market order flow. Their research concluded that factor crowding had elevated co-impact trading to the point where structural profits were pushed toward zero.

By mid-2026, quantitative strategists at JPMorgan reported that momentum factor crowding had reached the 100th percentile—the most extreme saturation observed in three decades, surging from the 25th percentile in just three months. While some academic literature suggests crowded momentum trades can temporarily suppress crash volatility during smooth uptrends, crowding turns into an exit bottleneck the moment trend directions reverse.

You can observe this failure directly in MTUM’s historical track record. In 2022, the fund tumbled 18.3%. In 2023, as the market staged an explosive recovery powered by emerging artificial intelligence trends, MTUM returned just 9.2% while the broad S&P 500 returned more than 26%. MTUM lagged the index by roughly 17 percentage points in a roaring bull market. Its rigid formula owned conservative defensive names left over from the 2022 bear market, not the tech leaders driving the recovery. During the pandemic panic of February and March 2020, MTUM plummeted 31.6%, matching the S&P 500’s 32% drawdown point-for-point.

The whipsaw mechanism is baked directly into the fund's reconstitution calendar. If the semiconductor industry suffers an inventory correction, chip stocks fall first. Because MTUM rebalances quarterly, its signals degrade after the price drop has occurred. The index then mechanically cuts those names at lower valuations and rotates into whatever defensive sector happened to hold up best over the preceding six to twelve months.

If tech promptly rebounds, the fund misses the recovery, stuck holding the newly purchased defensives. The hard 30% turnover cap exacerbates this lag, forcing the fund to drag stale positions across multiple quarters.

What would prove the bears entirely right is another year like 2023: double-digit underperformance during a market rally, driven by mechanical selling of beaten-down tech names immediately before they resume leadership. What would prove them wrong is an orderly, profitable transition in which MTUM smoothly trims semiconductors ahead of an extended cyclical slump and seamlessly captures an emerging trend in financial or industrial equities.

How to Use It

MTUM should never serve as the core engine of an equity portfolio. If you replace a standard broad-market S&P 500 or total market index fund with this ETF, you are not diversifying. You are swapping a balanced market basket for an aggressive sector tilt that historically experiences severe tracking errors and violent drawdowns.

Instead, MTUM functions as a tactical satellite holding. It belongs in a satellite sleeve, sized well below whatever you treat as a core holding, for an investor who actively wants momentum exposure but prefers an established institutional brand with high intraday liquidity.

Even within that narrow role, investors must ask what MTUM provides that its competitors do not. If your goal is factor-driven outperformance over five to ten years, SPMO’s simpler ranking methodology, wider rank buffers, and 44% turnover rate have historically extracted significantly more return with far less tax friction. If your goal is pure momentum without taking massive sector bets, sector-neutral funds like JMOM offer factor exposure without dumping half your money into Silicon Valley hardware.

MTUM suits investors who want cyclical, risk-adjusted tech exposure and plan to hold the shares in tax-sheltered accounts like an IRA or 401(k). Inside those accounts, 104% turnover never triggers an annual tax bite. It is completely unsuitable for taxable accounts, for conservative investors seeking factor diversification, or for anyone who expects a momentum fund to protect them during a sudden market downturn.

On November 5, 2026, MTUM will execute a 4-for-1 forward stock split, following a record date of November 3. The split will multiply your share count by four while reducing the share price by three-quarters, leaving the total economic value of your investment completely unchanged. It is a purely cosmetic change.

The real event to watch arrives at the close of the final business day of November. That is when the index implements its quarterly reconstitution. After an October that saw the fund drop 4.6% while the broader market advanced, the November review will reveal the answer. Does the turnover-capped algorithm double down on volatile chipmakers, or dump them into the pullback?

Analysis, not advice. We may own these names and we may sell them at any time.
